summary: Hamza Tahir opens by noting that while document auto-save has existed since the 1980s, AI agents still lack an equivalent. The closest thing today—traces—captures emitted telemetry (tool calls, inputs, outputs) but is disconnected from the actual runtime: variables in state, in-flight file systems, code decisions, and execution environment are all lost. This gap between observability spans and execution prevents meaningful post-hoc investigation. Tahir argues a checkpoint primitive solves this by snapshotting full system state—code, artifacts, environment (Docker images, sandboxes)—at each step. Once you have checkpoints, you can replay from any point: swap a model for a cheaper one, mock or override a tool's return value, or intentionally degrade behavior to test robustness. The core methodology is checkpoint, replay, diff, decide—take a cohort of production runs, replay a change, diff against the baseline, and route decisions back. This closes the loop on evaluation using production checkpoints rather than synthetic evals. A critical caution emerges: naive model swaps often create false economies. A BrainTrust study showed that cheaper models may look better on paper but fail to resolve requests, so you must evaluate value created, not just cost. Furthermore, a model passing 60% of the time is self-consistent only about a quarter of the time, meaning a single replay is merely an anecdote—cohort analysis across many runs is essential. The production playbook is to start from real production runs, build meaningful cohorts (expensive, long, risky ones), never ship based on one or two replays, automate the loop possibly with an agent, and keep a human in the loop. DoorDash is cited as doing this at scale, reducing iteration from hours to 5 minutes with 90% fewer hallucinations while staying within 2 points of production outcomes. The demo uses Kitaru, an open-source durable runtime from the ZenML team, showing a customer support agent handling chargeback disputes. Tahir views checkpoint details, replays from checkpoint 71 with GPT-5 Nano, mocks the lookup policy tool, and generates side-by-side diffs. Cohort replay across runs sorted by cost emits JSON reports analyzed via the Kitaru MCP server. The final verdict: don't ship the cheaper model—despite a promising single replay, cohort analysis showed it underperformed across many support cases. Kitaru is open source and free to use.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The Missing Save Button for Agents
sections.summary: Tahir introduces the core problem: agents lack a save button. Traces provide read-only telemetry but are disconnected from the runtime, losing variables, file systems, code, and environment state. A new stack category—durable runtimes below the harness layer—augments traces with full execution state to enable replay and what-if analysis.

sections.title: Closing the Eval Loop with Production Checkpoints
sections.summary: Checkpoints enable going back in time to ask what-if questions: swap models, mock tools, degrade behavior. The methodology is checkpoint, replay, diff, decide. DoorDash is cited as a successful example, reducing simulation time from hours to 5 minutes with 90% fewer hallucinations while staying within 2 points of production.

sections.title: Kitaru Demo: Single-Run Checkpoint Replay
sections.summary: Tahir demos Kitaru with a customer support agent handling chargeback disputes. He shows checkpoint details including config, execution location, code, and artifacts. He replays from checkpoint 71 with the model changed to GPT-5 Nano, demonstrating that prior checkpoints are skipped since their state is already captured.

sections.title: Kitaru Demo: Tool Mocking and Side-by-Side Diff
sections.summary: Tahir mocks the lookup policy tool with a different function while holding the model constant, producing a third run. The diff command generates a side-by-side comparison URL showing where execution diverged. All three runs restricted the charge, but the policy change shifted the outcome from needing review to safe-to-answer, at lower token cost.

sections.title: Cohort Replay and MCP-Based Analysis
sections.summary: Tahir extends to cohort replay—applying one change across many runs sorted by cost, emitting JSON reports. Because manual comparison of thousands of runs is infeasible, he uses the Kitaru MCP server to have an LLM analyze the cohort report and flag red flags, emphasizing that queryable runtimes and MCP integration are essential at scale.

sections.title: Cohort Verdict, Playbook, and Conclusion
sections.summary: Tahir warns that naive model swaps often create false economies, citing a BrainTrust study showing cheaper models may look better on paper but fail to resolve requests. He notes that a model passing 60% of the time is self-consistent only about 25% of the time, making single replays mere anecdotes. The production playbook: start from real runs, build meaningful cohorts (expensive, long, risky), never ship on 1-2 replays, automate the loop, keep a human in the loop. The demo's cohort verdict: don't ship the cheaper model despite promising single-replay results. Tahir concludes that agents need a harness and runtime that can checkpoint and replay state, and announces Kitaru is open source and free to use.
